Decreasing Forest Cover and its Impact on the Human Race

Long before cities and farms, humanity was born in the forest. Forests gave our ancestors food, shelter, medicine and fuel, and they still give every one of us the air we breathe and much of the water we drink. Yet the world continues to lose them. According to the Food and Agriculture Organization, about ten million hectares of forest are cut down every year — an area roughly the size of South Korea. In 2024 alone, fires and clearing destroyed a record area of tropical primary forest. The loss of forests is not only an environmental tragedy; it is a threat to the survival and well-being of the human race.

Why forests are disappearing

The main driver is the expansion of agriculture — cattle ranching and soya in the Amazon, oil palm in Indonesia and Malaysia, and shifting cultivation and encroachment elsewhere. Logging, mining, roads, dams and urban sprawl cut forests into fragments. Forest fires, made worse by heat and drought, now burn vast areas from Canada to Australia. Poverty, weak land rights and demand for cheap commodities in distant markets drive much of this destruction.

What the loss means for humanity

First, climate change. Forests store more carbon than the entire atmosphere. Deforestation releases this carbon and removes a sink that absorbs about a fifth to a quarter of the carbon dioxide we emit. Parts of the Amazon are close to a tipping point at which rainforest may turn into savanna and become a carbon source.

Second, water security. Forests regulate rainfall and river flow, recharge groundwater and protect catchments. When the hills are bare, rivers flood in the monsoon and run dry in summer. Mumbai's water comes from forested catchments; the Himalayan forests feed the rivers of the north Indian plains.

Third, disasters. Without tree roots, slopes slide and soils wash away. The landslides of Wayanad and the Himalaya, and the floods of Kerala, have been linked to the loss of forest and unplanned construction on fragile slopes. Mangroves protect coasts from cyclones and storm surges, as the Sundarbans and Bhitarkanika have shown.

Fourth, health. Clearing forests brings people and wildlife into closer contact and raises the risk of diseases that jump from animals to humans, such as Nipah and Ebola. Forests are also the source of many medicines, and smoke from forest fires kills thousands every year.

Fifth, livelihoods and culture. About 1.6 billion people worldwide, and an estimated 27 crore in India, depend on forests for food, fuel, fodder and income. For tribal communities, the forest is home, identity and the sacred. Their displacement is a human loss as well as an ecological one.

Finally, biodiversity. Forests hold most of the world's land species. The loss of pollinators, soil organisms and wild crop relatives threatens food security for all of us.

India's experience

India is one of the few countries where forest and tree cover has increased — to about a quarter of its area according to the India State of Forest Report 2023 — thanks to plantations, community efforts and agroforestry. Yet the quality of natural forests is a concern: dense forests are being degraded, the north-eastern States have lost cover, and plantations of a single species cannot replace natural forests rich in life. Large projects continue to divert forest land.

The way forward

  • Stop deforestation through strong laws, satellite monitoring and deforestation-free supply chains.
  • Secure the rights of forest communities, who are the best guardians of forests, under laws such as the Forest Rights Act.
  • Restore degraded land with native species: India has pledged to restore 26 million hectares by 2030.
  • Pay for ecosystem services, as India's Finance Commission does by giving weight to forest cover in sharing taxes with States.
  • Reduce consumption of products linked to deforestation, in the spirit of Mission LiFE.
  • Agroforestry and urban forests to meet timber needs and cool cities.

Conclusion

A Chinese proverb says that the best time to plant a tree was twenty years ago; the second-best time is now. The fate of forests and the fate of humanity are tied together. If we destroy forests, we destroy our own life-support system. If we protect and restore them, they will continue to give us air, water, food and stability for generations to come.

Need for Multidisciplinarity in Higher Education

The great problems of our time — climate change, pandemics, artificial intelligence, inequality — do not respect the walls between university departments. A climate scientist needs economics, an engineer designing AI needs ethics, and a doctor tackling a pandemic needs sociology and communication. Yet for decades Indian higher education has divided students early into rigid streams — science, commerce, arts — and kept them there. The need of the hour is multidisciplinarity.

What multidisciplinarity means

Multidisciplinary education allows students to study across fields: a physics student may take music, an engineering student philosophy, a history student data science. It also means research that brings different disciplines together to solve real problems. It is not new to India: ancient universities such as Takshashila and Nalanda taught grammar, medicine, logic, astronomy and the arts together, and the idea of the "64 kalas" combined many skills.

Why it is needed

First, complex problems need many lenses. Public health, sustainable cities and water management require science, technology, economics and social understanding together.

Second, the job market is changing. Automation is replacing routine tasks; employers value problem-solving, creativity, communication and the ability to learn new skills. A broad education prepares graduates for jobs that do not yet exist.

Third, innovation happens at the boundaries. Biotechnology, nanotechnology, behavioural economics and cognitive science were born when disciplines met.

Fourth, education for citizenship and character. The humanities and social sciences develop ethical reasoning, empathy and democratic values — essential when technology raises new moral questions.

Fifth, student choice and well-being. Rigid streams force teenagers to choose too early; flexibility lets them follow their interests and change course.

India's policy response

The National Education Policy 2020 makes multidisciplinarity central. It proposes large multidisciplinary universities and colleges, flexible four-year undergraduate programmes with multiple entry and exit options, an Academic Bank of Credits, and Multidisciplinary Education and Research Universities. The UGC's curriculum framework now allows students to combine major and minor subjects from different streams. IITs have added humanities and design departments; some new private universities follow the liberal-arts model.

Challenges

  • Faculty and infrastructure: most colleges are small and single-stream; affiliated colleges lack teachers in many subjects.
  • Mindsets: parents and students still value professional degrees and rank-based entrance examinations.
  • Assessment and recruitment: examinations and job criteria often reward narrow specialisation.
  • Risk of superficiality: breadth must not come at the cost of depth.
  • Funding: India spends far less on higher education and research than leading countries.

What should be done

  • Cluster small colleges into multidisciplinary institutions and allow credit transfer between them.
  • Train teachers for interdisciplinary teaching and support joint research centres.
  • Use online platforms such as SWAYAM to give students access to courses not available locally.
  • Reform entrance tests and recruitment to value broad learning.
  • Keep a balance: a strong major subject, with chosen minors and skills.

Conclusion

Rabindranath Tagore's Visva-Bharati sought an education in which art, science and life were one. In a world of rapid change, the most valuable graduates will be those who can connect ideas across fields and apply them with judgement and compassion. Multidisciplinarity is not a luxury but a necessity if Indian higher education is to produce thinkers, innovators and responsible citizens for a developed India.

Sports and Business

Sport was once seen as pure recreation and amateur passion. Today it is also big business. Football's World Cup, the Olympics and the Indian Premier League generate billions in broadcasting rights, sponsorships, merchandise and tourism. The relationship between sports and business is now inseparable — and it brings both great benefits and real dangers.

How business has transformed sport

The IPL is the clearest example in India. Its media rights for 2023–27 were sold for over ₹48,000 crore, making each match one of the most valuable sporting events in the world. Leagues in kabaddi, football, hockey and badminton have followed, giving players salaries and fame that were unthinkable a generation ago. Corporate sponsorship funds training, equipment and coaches. Private initiatives such as foundations and sports academies have supported Olympic medallists in shooting, wrestling, boxing and athletics.

Business has also brought professionalism: modern training, sports science, data analytics, nutrition and physiotherapy. Television and digital streaming have taken sport to every village, building new audiences and inspiring children. Sports tourism, infrastructure and ancillary industries — sports goods in Jalandhar and Meerut, fitness, apparel, gaming — create jobs and growth.

Sport as an engine for business

Sport is also a powerful brand-building tool. Companies use athletes to reach consumers; cities and countries host events to attract investment and tourism, as India hopes to do with its bid for the 2036 Olympics. The government sees sport as part of soft power and the economy through the Khelo India programme and the National Sports Policy.

The dark side

Commercialisation has costs.

  • Inequality between sports: cricket attracts most of the money, while many Olympic and traditional sports struggle.
  • Pressure on athletes: tight schedules, injuries and the demands of sponsors; young players may be exploited by agents.
  • Corruption and match-fixing: spot-fixing scandals in cricket and betting rackets damage the integrity of sport.
  • Gambling and fantasy gaming: aggressive marketing of real-money gaming, which India banned in 2025, raised concerns about addiction and debt.
  • Loss of the spirit of sport: when winning and profit dominate, values of fair play, community and joy may be lost; ticket prices may exclude ordinary fans.
  • Governance problems: sports bodies controlled by administrators with business or political interests.

Striking the right balance

  • Good governance: transparent, athlete-centred sports federations, as envisaged in the National Sports Governance Act, 2025.
  • Spread investment: corporate social responsibility and public funds for grassroots and less popular sports, women's sport and para-sports.
  • Protect integrity: strong laws against match-fixing, anti-doping and regulation of betting and gaming.
  • Protect athletes: fair contracts, player associations, insurance and career support after retirement.
  • Keep sport accessible: affordable facilities in schools and neighbourhoods.

Conclusion

Business has given sport money, reach and professionalism; sport has given business passion and loyalty. The partnership can make India a sporting nation and add to its economy — if it remains guided by fair play. Money should serve sport, not the other way round. As the Olympic motto reminds us, the aim is to be faster, higher, stronger — together.

Women's Safety at the Workplace

A workplace should be a place where every person can work with dignity and develop their talent. For many women in India, however, the workplace is also a place of fear — of harassment, discrimination and even violence. The brutal rape and murder of a young doctor at a hospital in Kolkata in August 2024 shocked the nation and showed that even the institutions meant to protect life can fail to protect the women who work there.

The scale of the problem

Women's safety at work includes freedom from sexual harassment, physical violence, unsafe working conditions and discrimination. Many cases go unreported because women fear losing their jobs, social stigma and slow processes. The problem is worse in the informal sector, where over 80% of working women are employed — domestic workers, construction labourers, agricultural workers and street vendors — who have little protection. Night shifts, poor transport and lack of basic facilities such as toilets and rest rooms add to the risk. Online harassment of women working in digital spaces is a newer threat.

The legal framework

The Supreme Court's Vishaka guidelines (1997) first recognised sexual harassment at the workplace as a violation of fundamental rights. They led to the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act). It requires every organisation with ten or more employees to set up an Internal Committee, and districts to have Local Committees for small and informal workplaces. Employers must create awareness and act on complaints within fixed timelines. The Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 punishes sexual harassment, stalking and assault. In Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa (2023), the Supreme Court found that many bodies had not even formed committees and directed strict compliance. The SHe-Box portal allows online complaints.

Gaps in implementation

  • Many workplaces, including government offices and hospitals, have no functioning committees.
  • Local Committees for the informal sector are often missing.
  • Members lack training; complainants fear retaliation.
  • Physical safety — lighting, CCTV, security, safe transport — is neglected.
  • A workplace culture that tolerates sexist behaviour silences women.

What must be done

  • Strict enforcement: audits of POSH compliance, penalties for employers who fail, and reporting in annual reports.
  • Safe infrastructure: well-lit premises, rest rooms, CCTV in public areas, security staff, and safe transport for night shifts. After the Kolkata case, the Supreme Court set up a National Task Force on the safety of medical professionals.
  • Informal sector protection: functional Local Committees, women's helplines (181) and One Stop Centres.
  • Gender-sensitisation training for all employees and leaders, and more women in leadership positions.
  • Quick justice: fast-track courts and police sensitivity.
  • Change in social attitudes through education from school onwards.

Why it matters

Women's safety is not only a matter of rights; it is essential for the economy. India's female labour-force participation is still low, and fear of harassment and unsafe travel is one reason women leave or avoid jobs. A safe workplace attracts and retains talent, raises productivity and builds trust.

Conclusion

Swami Vivekananda said that it is impossible to think about the welfare of the world unless the condition of women is improved. A truly developed India must be one where a woman can work in a hospital, a factory, a farm or an office at any hour without fear. Laws exist; what is needed now is the will to enforce them and a culture of respect in every workplace.

Poaching on the Rise in Wildlife Sanctuaries

XYZ, from our correspondent

Rising incidents of poaching in India's wildlife sanctuaries and national parks have alarmed conservationists and forest officials.

Data from wildlife monitoring groups show that dozens of tigers and leopards die every year due to poaching, while pangolins, star tortoises, birds and marine species are increasingly smuggled. Last month, forest officials seized tiger skins and bones from a gang operating near a reserve in central India. In another sanctuary, a forest guard was injured in a clash with armed poachers.

Officials say the main drivers are the international illegal trade in wildlife parts, used in traditional medicines and as luxury goods, and local demand for bushmeat. Poachers often use snares, electrocution from live wires and poison, and organised networks smuggle parts across borders.

"Our staff are few and the areas are large. Many posts of forest guards are vacant," said a senior forest officer of the ABC sanctuary.

Experts point to gaps such as shortage of frontline staff, lack of modern equipment and slow court cases. They have called for more patrolling with drones and camera traps, intelligence-sharing through the Wildlife Crime Control Bureau, faster prosecution under the Wildlife (Protection) Act, and involving local communities as informers and protectors.

Officials say a special drive with joint patrols of police and forest staff will begin soon in vulnerable reserves.

The line between drinks and food is blurred: a milkshake can contain five times the calories of the same ice cream eaten as dessert, yet we treat it as only a drink and eat a full meal with it.

Calorie-rich drinks, soft and alcoholic, have contributed greatly to excessive energy intake. Many people no longer recognise simple thirst for water, and a vast range of beverages, including sugary drinks posing as healthy, now contain as many calories as food. Culturally we do not see liquids as food, and the drinks industry has persuaded us that every occasion needs a drink.

Our biology, however, has not adapted to high-calorie drinks. The real problem is not only sugar but that liquids do not satisfy hunger. Studies show that people do not eat less after consuming calories in drinks, which pass quickly and barely reduce hunger. Even milk-based drinks fill us up less than equivalent food. As a result, we consume far more energy from drinks than we intend or realise.

Samudragupta (c. 335–375 CE) built the Gupta Empire into the leading power of India. Most of what we know comes from the Allahabad (Prayaga) Pillar inscription composed by his court poet Harisena, and from his coins.

1. As a statesman

  • Aryavarta (north India): he "uprooted" nine kings and annexed their lands — direct rule over the Ganga valley.
  • Dakshinapatha (south): he defeated twelve rulers, including Vishnugopa of Kanchi, but restored them as tributaries — the policy of grahana-moksha-anugraha (capture, release and favour). This avoided overstretching the empire.
  • Forest kingdoms (atavika rajyas) of central India were made his servants, securing the route south.
  • Frontier states (Samatata, Kamarupa, Nepal) and tribal republics (Malavas, Yaudheyas) paid tribute.
  • Distant rulers such as the Kushana "Daivaputra Shahi Shahanushahi", the Shakas and the king of Simhala sent embassies and gifts.
  • He performed the Ashvamedha sacrifice and issued Ashvamedha coins to proclaim paramountcy.

V.A. Smith called him the "Indian Napoleon"; unlike Napoleon, he knew where to stop and used diplomacy.

2. As an administrator

  • A centralised core with a feudatory ring outside — a flexible model later Indian empires used.
  • Officials such as mahadandanayaka, sandhivigrahika (minister of war and peace — Harisena held this post) and kumaramatya.
  • Gold coins (dinaras) of fine quality showing prosperity; the "lyrist" type shows him playing the veena.
  • Patron of culture: a poet himself (Kaviraja), patron of Sanskrit learning; he followed Vaishnavism yet tolerated Buddhism (he allowed the king of Sri Lanka to build a monastery at Bodh Gaya).

3. Critical evaluation

  • The inscription is a court eulogy and exaggerates; little is known of his civil administration.
  • The southern "conquest" was a raid more than lasting rule.

Still, Samudragupta combined military skill with realistic statecraft and laid the foundation of the Gupta "classical age".

Gautama Buddha and Vardhamana Mahavira were contemporaries of the 6th–5th century BCE who belonged to the shramana (ascetic) tradition that questioned Brahmanical orthodoxy.

Similarities in their teachings

  • Rejection of Vedic authority and ritual: both denied that animal sacrifices and priestly rituals could bring salvation.
  • Opposition to caste-based superiority: both admitted people of all varnas and stressed conduct over birth.
  • Ahimsa (non-violence): both made non-injury to living beings central; Mahavira took it further.
  • Karma and rebirth: both accepted that actions decide future births and that the cycle of rebirth is suffering.
  • Liberation through personal effort: nirvana (Buddha) and kaivalya/moksha (Mahavira) were to be gained by right conduct and knowledge, not by God's grace; neither gave importance to a creator god.
  • Ethical life: truth, non-stealing, non-attachment and self-control (the Jain mahavratas, the Buddha's panchashila).
  • Monastic orders: both founded orders (sangha) of monks and nuns with lay followers.
  • People's language: both preached in Prakrit languages — Pali (Buddha) and Ardhamagadhi (Mahavira).
  • Royal patronage from rulers of Magadha such as Bimbisara and Ajatashatru.

Both teachings made Indian religion more ethical, egalitarian and non-violent, and influenced later thinkers including Gandhi.

The rise of the Marathas was a major cause of Mughal decline, but it was one of several causes.

How the Marathas weakened the Mughals

  • The Deccan ulcer: Aurangzeb spent his last 26 years (1681–1707) fighting in the Deccan against the Marathas, draining treasury and armies.
  • Guerrilla warfare: under Shivaji, Sambhaji, Rajaram and Tarabai the Marathas wore down Mughal armies.
  • Expansion after 1707: the Peshwas (Baji Rao I) took Malwa, Gujarat and Bundelkhand, collected chauth and sardeshmukhi, and raided Delhi (1737). By the 1750s the Mughal emperor depended on them.

Other causes

  • Weak successors after 1707 and wars of succession.
  • Crisis of the jagirdari system: too few jagirs for too many mansabdars.
  • Court factions (Irani, Turani, Hindustani) and the rise of independent provinces — Hyderabad, Bengal, Awadh.
  • Revolts of Jats, Sikhs and Rajputs; agrarian distress.
  • Foreign invasions: Nadir Shah (1739) and Ahmad Shah Abdali.
  • European companies, especially the English after Plassey (1757).

The Marathas hastened the decline, but the empire was already weakened from within.

Limits: they were largely urban and upper-caste in the beginning, and some revivalist strands deepened communal identities.

India's female labour force participation rate has risen to about 41.7% (PLFS 2023-24), but it remains well below the global average of about 50%, and much of the increase is in unpaid or self-employed farm work.

1. Why female employment is low

  • Social norms: marriage, purdah, and the belief that a woman's place is at home; the "income effect" — as household incomes rise, women withdraw from manual work.
  • Unpaid care work: Indian women spend about five hours a day on unpaid domestic and care work, several times more than men (Time Use Survey).
  • Lack of suitable jobs: few non-farm jobs in rural areas; mechanisation of agriculture displaced women.
  • Safety and mobility: harassment and poor transport limit travel to work.
  • Education–skill mismatch and the wage gap; few jobs close to home.
  • Measurement: much of women's work is unpaid and not counted.

2. Steps to boost women's participation

  • Care infrastructure: creches under the Maternity Benefit Act, anganwadi-cum-creches (Palna scheme), elder care.
  • Safe workplaces and transport: strict enforcement of the POSH Act, safe public transport, working women's hostels (SAKHI Niwas).
  • Jobs near home: labour-intensive manufacturing (garments, electronics assembly), MGNREGA, food processing and the care economy.
  • Skilling and credit: Skill India, self-help groups (Lakhpati Didi), Stand-Up India and Mudra loans.
  • Flexible work: part-time, remote and gig work with social security under the labour codes.
  • Equal pay and changed norms: enforcing equal remuneration, paternity leave and campaigns for shared care.

Raising women's participation is also an economic opportunity: estimates suggest that closing the gender gap in work could add significantly to India's GDP.

Manufacturing as the engine of growth

  • It has higher productivity than agriculture and absorbs low- and semi-skilled labour — the path taken by East Asian economies.
  • It has strong linkages with services, mining and agriculture, and drives exports and technology.
  • Economies of scale and innovation raise growth over the long run.

Why India has not succeeded enough

Manufacturing has stayed at about 15–17% of GDP for decades, far short of the 25% goal of the National Manufacturing Policy (2011) and Make in India.

  • Infrastructure and logistics costs were high (though falling with the PM Gati Shakti plan).
  • Rigid labour laws in the past and land acquisition delays.
  • Small firms that do not grow — "missing middle".
  • Costly credit, power and compliance; inverted duty structures.
  • Weak skills and low spending on R&D (about 0.65% of GDP).
  • Competition from China and limited integration into global value chains.

Policies recommended

  • Implement the labour codes and simplify land and approvals at State level.
  • Continue PLI schemes (14 sectors) and support electronics, semiconductors and green technology.
  • Logistics reform (National Logistics Policy, 2022) and industrial corridors with plug-and-play parks.
  • MSME support: cheaper credit, formalisation, the TReDS platform for payments.
  • Skilling linked to industry; more R&D.
  • Trade policy: lower tariffs on inputs, free-trade agreements to join global value chains.

A competitive, labour-intensive manufacturing base is essential if India is to provide jobs for its young workforce.

TariffsGlobal value chainsExport-led growthFriend-shoring

Protectionism — tariffs, import quotas and subsidies to protect domestic industry — has risen worldwide: the US–China trade war since 2018, US tariffs on many partners in 2025, and "buy local" policies.

Adverse effects on emerging economies

  • Lower exports and growth: emerging economies depend on access to large markets; tariffs reduce demand.
  • Broken value chains raise costs for firms that import inputs.
  • Less investment and technology transfer.
  • Retaliation and uncertainty slow world trade; the WTO's dispute system has been weakened.

The other side

  • Some emerging economies gain from trade diversion (China-plus-one): Vietnam, Mexico and India attract firms leaving China.
  • Limited, targeted protection can help build infant industries (as with India's electronics PLI).
  • Large domestic markets such as India's reduce dependence on exports.

On balance, rising protectionism hurts emerging economies as a group, but those with good policies can turn supply-chain shifts into opportunities through trade agreements and competitiveness.

Money supplyDemand-pull inflationRepo rateFiscal deficit

How excess liquidity causes inflation

When there is more money in the economy than the goods and services available, people and firms spend more. This demand-pull pressure pushes up prices in general — "too much money chasing too few goods". Cheap credit also fuels asset prices and inflation expectations.

Which policy is more effective?

  • Monetary policy is usually more effective and faster for demand-pull inflation. The RBI can raise the repo rate, increase the CRR, and absorb liquidity through the Standing Deposit Facility and open market sales. India's inflation-targeting framework (4% ± 2%) gives it a clear mandate.
  • Fiscal policy — lower deficits, less borrowing, reduced subsidies — reduces demand, but it is slow and politically hard; it is better for supply-side inflation (cutting taxes on fuel, releasing food stocks, import duty changes).

Both work best together: monetary policy for demand pressure, fiscal and supply measures for food and fuel shocks.

Social revolutionFundamental RightsDirective PrinciplesGranville Austin

Granville Austin called the Indian Constitution "first and foremost a social document", and said that Parts III and IV are its "conscience". Together they aim at a peaceful social revolution — moving from a hierarchical, unequal society to one based on liberty, equality and justice.

1. Part III: Fundamental Rights

  • Equality: Article 14 (equality before law), Article 15 (no discrimination, with special provisions for women, children and backward classes), Article 16 (equal opportunity and reservation).
  • Abolition of untouchability (Article 17) and titles (Article 18).
  • Freedoms (Article 19) and protection of life and liberty (Article 21), now read to include dignity, livelihood, education (21A) and privacy.
  • Against exploitation: ban on trafficking and forced labour (Article 23) and child labour (Article 24).
  • Cultural and educational rights of minorities (Articles 29–30).
  • Article 32 — the "heart and soul" (Ambedkar) — makes these rights enforceable.

2. Part IV: Directive Principles of State Policy

  • Social and economic justice (Article 38); distribution of resources and prevention of concentration of wealth (Article 39(b), (c)).
  • Equal pay, living wage, humane conditions of work (Articles 39, 42, 43).
  • Free legal aid (39A), village panchayats (40), right to work and education (41, 45), welfare of weaker sections (46), health and nutrition (47).

3. How they work together

  • Minerva Mills (1980): harmony and balance between Parts III and IV is a basic feature.
  • Laws on land reform, minimum wages, MGNREGA, the Right to Education and the Food Security Act turned DPSPs into rights.

The Constitution thus uses enforceable rights to protect individuals and directive principles to guide the State towards a just society — a revolution through law rather than violence.
free.ifm-2024-gk-3b:

The basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits Parliament's power to amend the Constitution. Most of the cases that shaped it turned on two values — democracy and rights.

1. Democracy

  • Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975): the 39th Amendment, which put the Prime Minister's election beyond judicial review, was struck down; free and fair elections are part of the basic structure.
  • Kihoto Hollohan (1992): the anti-defection law upheld but the Speaker's decision made subject to judicial review.
  • S.R. Bommai (1994): federalism and secularism held basic features; misuse of Article 356 checked.
  • NJAC case (2015): the 99th Amendment was struck down to protect judicial independence, a pillar of constitutional democracy.

2. Rights

  • Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights but cannot destroy their essence.
  • Minerva Mills (1980): limited amending power and the balance between Parts III and IV are basic features; Article 31C's wide extension struck down.
  • Waman Rao (1981) and I.R. Coelho (2007): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be tested against the rights in Articles 14, 19 and 21.
  • M. Nagaraj (2006): equality is part of the basic structure.
  • Janhit Abhiyan (2022): the EWS amendment upheld, showing that the doctrine is applied carefully.

3. Assessment

The statement is justified: the doctrine has been used to protect democratic processes and the core of rights from majoritarian amendment. Critics call it judicial overreach and point to its vagueness; supporters see it as the guardian of constitutionalism.

India's Constitution provides for representative democracy: people elect representatives to Parliament, State legislatures and local bodies, and governments are responsible to these legislatures. There is no provision for a national referendum, initiative or recall.

Strengths of the representative form

  • Suitable for a large, diverse country; it allows deliberation and protects minorities from majority impulses.
  • Regular, free elections conducted by an independent Election Commission; universal adult franchise.
  • Accountability through question hour, committees and no-confidence motions.

Elements of direct democracy that exist

  • Gram Sabhas under the 73rd Amendment and PESA, 1996; some States allow recall of panchayat heads.
  • Public consultation, RTI, social audits of MGNREGA, and public interest litigation.

Weaknesses

  • Money and muscle power, criminalisation, weak internal party democracy and declining legislative sittings.

Indian democracy is therefore representative at its core but has been deepened by participatory tools at the local level.

The State Election Commission (SEC), created by the 73rd and 74th Amendments (Articles 243K and 243ZA), conducts elections to panchayats and municipalities.

A channel of political expression at the local level

  • Regular elections to about 2.6 lakh panchayats and thousands of urban bodies give citizens a direct voice in local affairs.
  • Reservation for SCs, STs, OBCs and at least one-third (in many States half) for women brings new groups into politics.
  • It prepares voter lists, delimits wards and enforces the model code.

Reconciling people's desires and regional democratic needs

  • Kishansing Tomar (2006): elections must be held on time; the SEC can approach courts if the State delays.
  • SECs adapt to local conditions — different reservation rosters, rotation of seats, tribal areas (PESA).
  • Courts have backed the SEC's independence; the Suresh Mahajan (2022) case required timely local elections even when OBC data was pending.

Problems: delays by State governments, dependence on States for staff and money, and weak powers compared with the Election Commission of India. Giving SECs real autonomy would strengthen grassroots democracy.

Burst of monsoonITCZKharifWater security

The south-west monsoon does not arrive gradually; it bursts suddenly over Kerala around 1 June and covers the country by about 8 July. This sudden onset — the "burst of the monsoon" — follows the northward shift of the ITCZ, the reversal of winds and the arrival of the easterly jet and the moisture-laden south-westerlies.

Climatic significance

  • Sudden change from hot, dry summer to heavy rain and lower temperatures.
  • Provides about 75% of India's annual rainfall in four months.
  • Controls the seasons: the rainy season, followed by the retreating monsoon.

Socio-economic significance

  • Agriculture: kharif sowing of rice, pulses, cotton and oilseeds depends on timely onset; about half of net sown area is rain-fed.
  • Water: reservoirs, groundwater and rivers are recharged; drinking water and hydropower.
  • Economy: rural incomes, food prices and inflation follow the monsoon; it is called the "real finance minister".
  • Culture: festivals and the farming calendar are tied to it.
  • Disasters: a sudden burst can cause floods and landslides; a delayed or weak onset brings drought.

The abrupt arrival of the monsoon therefore shapes the life, economy and culture of the subcontinent; changing monsoon behaviour under climate change makes forecasting and water management even more important.

Causes of the changing urban environment

  • Land-use change: forests, wetlands and farms are replaced by concrete, asphalt and buildings.
  • Population and economic activity: more vehicles, industries, air-conditioners and energy use.
  • Waste generation: solid waste, sewage and industrial effluents beyond treatment capacity.
  • Loss of water bodies and green spaces due to encroachment.
  • Vertical growth that blocks winds.
  • Climate change adding heat waves and extreme rainfall.

How the urban environment differs from non-urban areas

Consequences: urban flooding (Chennai, Bengaluru), heat stress, respiratory disease and water scarcity.

Remedies: green and blue infrastructure, better public transport, waste segregation and recycling, protection of lakes and wetlands, and climate-resilient urban planning.

Responsible tourismLocal communitiesConservation awarenessCultural integrity

Eco-tourism is responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, sustains local people and involves learning.

Ecological consciousness

  • Visitors see wildlife and fragile ecosystems first-hand — tiger reserves, mangroves, the Western Ghats — and learn why they must be conserved.
  • Rules on waste, noise and carrying capacity teach responsible behaviour.
  • Entry fees fund conservation (Periyar Tiger Reserve's eco-development model).

Social consciousness

  • Community-based tourism: homestays in Sikkim and Ladakh, tribal guides and village eco-development committees give local people income and a stake in conservation.
  • Reduces dependence on forest extraction and poaching.

Cultural integrity

  • Tourists experience local cuisine, crafts, festivals and traditional knowledge (for example the sacred groves of Meghalaya and the Bishnoi villages of Rajasthan), which gives communities pride in their culture.
  • Revenue supports crafts and performing arts.

Caution: unregulated tourism can commercialise culture and harm ecosystems, as in some Himalayan towns. Eco-tourism must follow carrying-capacity limits and give local people control.

Chromite (FeCr2O4) is the only ore of chromium.

Distribution in India

  • Odisha holds over 90% of India's resources, mainly in the Sukinda valley (Jajpur) and also Dhenkanal and Keonjhar — one of the world's major chromite belts.
  • Smaller deposits in Karnataka (Hassan, Mysuru), Andhra Pradesh (Krishna district — Kondapalli), Jharkhand (Singhbhum), Maharashtra (Bhandara), Manipur and Nagaland.

Socio-economic significance

  • Ferrochrome and stainless steel: chromium gives steel hardness and corrosion resistance; India is a major ferrochrome producer and exporter.
  • Refractories for furnaces, and chemicals for tanning, pigments and electroplating.
  • Strategic and defence uses in alloys for aircraft and weapons.
  • Jobs and revenue in Odisha; royalty and the District Mineral Foundation fund local development.

Concerns: Sukinda is among the world's most polluted places because hexavalent chromium contaminates water, causing disease. Safe mining, effluent treatment and health care for local tribal communities are essential.

Composition of biogas

Biogas is produced by anaerobic digestion of cattle dung, crop residue, food waste and sewage. It contains:

  • Methane (CH4): 50–70% — the fuel component;
  • Carbon dioxide (CO2): 30–40%;
  • small amounts of hydrogen sulphide, nitrogen, hydrogen and water vapour.

When purified to over 90% methane it becomes compressed biogas (CBG), similar to CNG.

Government efforts

  • National Biogas and Manure Management Programme (since 1981-82) for family-size plants; now part of the National Bioenergy Programme (2021-26) with subsidies for biogas plants.
  • GOBARdhan (2018) under Swachh Bharat Mission (Grameen) to turn cattle dung and organic waste into biogas and organic manure; a unified registration portal.
  • SATAT (2018): oil companies buy CBG at assured prices; target of 5,000 CBG plants.
  • CBG Blending Obligation: 1% CBG in CNG and piped gas from 2025-26, rising to 5% by 2028-29.
  • Financial support: priority-sector lending, Central Financial Assistance, and the Market Development Assistance for fermented organic manure.
  • Waste-to-energy plants in cities under the Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban).

Benefits: clean cooking fuel, less dependence on LPG and gas imports, lower methane emissions and organic manure for soils.

Challenges: high cost of plants, feedstock collection and low demand for slurry; viable business models and FPO-led plants can help.

Recombinant DNAInsulinVaccinesGene therapy

Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology joins DNA from different sources and inserts it into a host (bacteria, yeast or mammalian cells) so that the host makes a desired product.

Benefits for healthcare and pharmaceutics

  • Therapeutic proteins: human insulin (the first rDNA drug, 1982), growth hormone, erythropoietin, interferons and clotting factors for haemophilia — safer and cheaper than animal-derived products.
  • Vaccines: the hepatitis B vaccine made in yeast; HPV and some COVID-19 vaccines use recombinant proteins or vectors.
  • Monoclonal antibodies for cancer and autoimmune diseases.
  • Diagnostics: recombinant antigens in test kits; PCR and DNA probes for infections and genetic disorders.
  • Gene therapy: inserting correct genes to treat inherited diseases; CAR-T cell therapy for cancer (India's NexCAR19, 2023).
  • Drug discovery: producing target proteins for testing drugs; transgenic animals as disease models.
  • Biosimilars: India is a major producer of affordable biosimilars.

Concerns: biosafety, high cost of some therapies and ethical issues, regulated in India by the Review Committee on Genetic Manipulation and the CDSCO.

rDNA technology has made many life-saving medicines safe, plentiful and affordable.

Vermicomposting is the conversion of organic waste — crop residue, cattle dung, kitchen waste — into nutrient-rich manure (vermicompost) with the help of earthworms such as Eisenia fetida and Eudrilus eugeniae.

Importance for sustainable agriculture

  • Soil health: adds organic matter, improves soil structure, aeration and water-holding capacity.
  • Nutrients: rich in nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, micronutrients and plant-growth hormones; reduces chemical fertiliser use.
  • Beneficial microbes that suppress some plant diseases.
  • Waste recycling: converts farm and urban waste into a resource, reducing burning and landfills.
  • Low cost and income: farmers and women's SHGs can produce and sell vermicompost.
  • Supports organic and natural farming (Paramparagat Krishi Vikas Yojana, National Mission on Natural Farming) and better crop quality.

Vermicomposting is thus a simple, eco-friendly way to restore soil fertility and make farming sustainable.

Extreme rainfallWarmer atmosphereUrban floodsLandslides

India is seeing fewer moderate rain days and more heavy and extreme rain events. Studies show a roughly threefold rise in widespread extreme rainfall events over central India between 1950 and 2015.

Causes

  • Warmer air holds more moisture — about 7% more for every 1 °C rise (Clausius–Clapeyron relation), so storms dump more water.
  • Warming of the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean increases moisture supply.
  • Changes in monsoon circulation and longer dry spells between bursts.
  • Urbanisation: heat islands and aerosols intensify local rain.
  • Western disturbances interacting with the monsoon in the Himalayas.

Consequences

  • Floods and urban flooding: Mumbai, Chennai, Bengaluru and Delhi.
  • Landslides and flash floods in the Himalayas and Western Ghats (Wayanad, 2024).
  • Crop damage, soil erosion and lower groundwater recharge because water runs off quickly.
  • Loss of lives, infrastructure and livelihoods; health risks from waterborne disease.

Responses: better forecasting and early warning, sponge-city design, protecting wetlands and drains, slope stabilisation and climate-resilient agriculture.

PM Surya Ghar: Muft Bijli Yojana (approved February 2024) aims to install rooftop solar on one crore households with an outlay of about ₹75,021 crore up to 2026-27.

Main features

  • Up to 300 units of free electricity a month for participating households.
  • Central Financial Assistance: ₹30,000 per kW for the first 2 kW and ₹18,000 for the third kW, up to ₹78,000 for a 3 kW system.
  • Collateral-free loans at low interest for systems up to 3 kW.
  • A national portal for applications, vendor selection and subsidy transfer directly to bank accounts.
  • Net metering: surplus power is sold to the DISCOM.
  • A model solar village in every district; incentives to DISCOMs and local bodies.

Merits of rooftop solar

  • Lower electricity bills; extra income from surplus power.
  • Clean energy: cuts emissions and fossil-fuel imports; helps meet 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030.
  • No land needed; reduces transmission losses as power is generated where it is used.
  • Creates local jobs in installation and maintenance.

Demerits

  • High upfront cost without subsidy; roof space and shade problems in cities and for tenants.
  • Intermittent supply — no power at night without storage.
  • Grid management problems for DISCOMs with many small generators; delays in net-metering.
  • Quality of panels and after-sales service; disposal of panels at end of life.

With storage, smart meters and better DISCOM finances, rooftop solar can make households energy producers.

Liquid crystalsPolarisationLED backlightOLED

1. Working principle of an LCD

  • Liquid crystals are materials whose molecules can flow like a liquid but stay aligned like a crystal.
  • An LCD panel has a backlight, two polarising filters at right angles, and a layer of liquid crystals between glass plates with transparent electrodes.
  • With no voltage, the twisted liquid crystals rotate the light's polarisation by 90°, so light passes through the second filter — the pixel is bright.
  • When a voltage is applied, the crystals straighten, the light is not rotated and is blocked — the pixel is dark.
  • Colour filters (red, green, blue) in each pixel and a thin-film transistor (TFT) for each sub-pixel create the image.

2. LED TVs

An "LED TV" is an LCD TV with an LED backlight instead of fluorescent tubes (CCFL). LEDs may be at the edges (edge-lit) or behind the panel in zones (full-array local dimming), which gives deeper blacks. QLED adds a quantum-dot layer for richer colours. OLED TVs are different: each pixel is an organic LED that emits its own light, so no backlight is needed.

3. Main difference between LCD and LED TVs

So the image-forming technology is the same; the difference lies in the backlight, which makes LED TVs thinner, brighter and more energy-efficient.

PolygraphPhysiological responsesSelvi caseReliability

Basic principle

A lie detector (polygraph) test assumes that lying causes stress, which produces involuntary physiological changes. The polygraph records:

  • blood pressure and pulse,
  • breathing rate,
  • skin conductance (sweating — galvanic skin response).

The examiner compares responses to relevant questions with control questions; larger changes are taken as signs of deception.

Factors affecting results

  • Anxiety or fear in innocent persons gives false positives.
  • Trained or calm liars, drugs and countermeasures (controlled breathing, pain) give false negatives.
  • Medical conditions (heart disease, high blood pressure) and fatigue.
  • Examiner's skill, question design and interpretation.
  • Environment and the subject's language and culture.

Legal position in India: in Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010), the Supreme Court held that polygraph, narco-analysis and brain-mapping cannot be done without consent (Articles 20(3) and 21); results are not admissible as evidence on their own, though information discovered with consent may be used. Because of these limits, such tests are only investigative aids.

Zero tailpipe emissionBattery costCharging infrastructurePM E-DRIVE

Merits of electric vehicles (EVs)

  • No tailpipe emissions: cleaner city air; lower greenhouse emissions as the grid gets greener.
  • Lower running and maintenance costs: electricity is cheaper than petrol and EVs have fewer moving parts.
  • Energy security: less dependence on imported oil.
  • Quiet, efficient (about 80–90% efficiency, against about 25–30% for petrol engines).

Demerits

  • High upfront cost, mainly of the battery.
  • Charging infrastructure is limited; long charging times and "range anxiety".
  • Battery minerals (lithium, cobalt, nickel) are imported and their mining harms the environment; battery recycling is still weak.
  • Emissions shift to coal-based power unless the grid becomes cleaner.
  • Fire-safety concerns.

Future prospects

  • EV sales in India crossed about 2 million in 2024-25, led by two- and three-wheelers.
  • Policies: FAME and now PM E-DRIVE (2024), PLI for advanced chemistry cell batteries and auto parts, lower GST (5%) on EVs, battery-swapping and charging standards, the National Critical Mineral Mission (2025).
  • Falling battery prices, sodium-ion batteries and electric buses under the PM e-Bus Sewa scheme point to rapid growth.

With clean power, local battery manufacturing and charging networks, EVs can transform transport in India.
free.ifm-2025-ge-1a:
Children in warTraumaEducation under fireProtection

Childhood in Conflict Zones

A child in Gaza who counts drones instead of stars, a girl in Sudan who walks for days to a camp, a boy in eastern Ukraine who has spent two winters in a basement classroom — these are not rare stories. According to UNICEF, more than 470 million children, about one in six in the world, live in areas affected by conflict. Childhood, which should be a time of play, learning and safety, has become for them a time of fear, loss and survival.

What war takes from children

The most visible loss is life and limb. The UN's annual report on children and armed conflict now records more than 30,000 grave violations against children in a single year: killing and maiming, recruitment as soldiers, abduction, sexual violence, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian aid. Landmines and unexploded shells continue to kill children long after the guns fall silent.

War also destroys the systems that protect children. Schools are bombed or turned into shelters and barracks; teachers flee; examinations stop. Hospitals lose power and medicine, and vaccination campaigns collapse, so measles and polio return. Families are torn apart. Millions of children are displaced — they grow up in camps, cross borders alone, and fall prey to traffickers. Hunger follows conflict closely: famine conditions in parts of Sudan and Gaza have left children with stunted bodies and minds.

The deepest wound is often invisible. Children who have seen killing, lost parents or lived under bombardment carry trauma — nightmares, anxiety, aggression and withdrawal. Without care, this toxic stress affects brain development, learning and relationships for life. Child soldiers face a double burden: they are both victims and, in the eyes of their communities, perpetrators.

A lost generation and a cycle of violence

When a generation grows up without education, without health and with grief and anger, the cost falls on the whole society. Illiteracy, unemployment and resentment make young people easy recruits for armed groups, and the conflict feeds itself. Peace becomes harder, because reconciliation requires citizens who can imagine a future different from their past.

What exists to protect children

The world has built a framework. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989), the most widely ratified human-rights treaty, and its Optional Protocol on children in armed conflict set 18 as the minimum age for direct participation in hostilities. International humanitarian law protects civilians, schools and hospitals. The Safe Schools Declaration commits states to keep schools out of military use. The UN Security Council's monitoring of "six grave violations" names the parties that harm children.

Yet these rules are often ignored. Accountability is weak, aid is blocked, and humanitarian appeals for education in emergencies receive only a small share of what is needed.

What must be done

First, prevention and accountability: parties to conflict must respect international law, and those who target children must face justice through national courts and international mechanisms.

Second, education cannot wait. Temporary learning spaces, radio and digital lessons, and teachers trained for crisis settings can keep learning alive. Education gives children routine, hope and protection from recruitment.

Third, mental-health and psychosocial support must be part of every humanitarian response — child-friendly spaces, trained counsellors and family tracing to reunite separated children.

Fourth, reintegration of former child soldiers through schooling, skills training and community acceptance, as tried in Sierra Leone and Colombia.

Fifth, funding and access: humanitarian corridors and predictable funding for nutrition, health and education.

India too has a role. Children in conflict-affected parts of our own country — in areas affected by insurgency or ethnic violence such as Manipur — need special care through schools, Child Welfare Committees under the Juvenile Justice Act and relief camps that respect their needs. Abroad, India's humanitarian aid and peacekeeping, where Indian troops and the women's units have protected civilians, show what responsible engagement can do.

Conclusion

Nelson Mandela said that there can be no keener revelation of a society's soul than the way in which it treats its children. Conflict zones reveal how often adults fail that test. Protecting childhood in war is not charity; it is an investment in peace. Every school kept open, every child reunited with a parent and every young mind helped to heal is a step towards ending the cycle of violence. The children who survive today's wars will build — or break — tomorrow's peace.
free.ifm-2025-ge-1b:
DevelopmentWildlifeCoexistenceSustainable growth

Wildlife Preservation and the Development Drive

India is one of the world's seventeen mega-diverse countries. With only 2.4% of the world's land, it holds about 7–8% of recorded species, including the largest populations of wild tigers and Asian elephants. India is also the world's most populous country and one of the fastest-growing major economies, building roads, railways, dams, mines and cities at great speed. The question of our time is whether these two facts can live together.

Why development presses on wildlife

Development needs land, water and energy. Highways and railway lines cut through forests and elephant corridors; hundreds of elephants have died on railway tracks in recent decades. Mining for coal, iron and bauxite removes forests in central India, the heart of tiger and elephant habitat. Dams submerge valleys, and urban growth swallows wetlands and grasslands. Habitat loss and fragmentation, rather than hunting, are now the biggest threats to wildlife. When habitats shrink, human–wildlife conflict rises: leopards in Mumbai's suburbs, elephants in Kerala's villages and tigers near farms in Maharashtra.

Why wildlife matters for development

Wildlife is not a luxury standing in the way of growth. Forests and wild areas provide water for rivers and cities, protect soil, store carbon and pollinate crops. Kaziranga's floodplains, the Sundarbans' mangroves and the Western Ghats' forests protect millions of people from floods, cyclones and drought. Wildlife tourism supports local jobs. Development that destroys these services is not development at all; it simply shifts costs onto the poor and the future.

India's record

India has shown that conservation can succeed even with large populations. Project Tiger (1973) has helped tiger numbers rise to over 3,600 (2022 estimate), about three-quarters of the world's wild tigers. The Asiatic lion has recovered in Gir; the one-horned rhino in Kaziranga. Laws such as the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest Conservation Act, 1980, and a network of over a thousand protected areas, provide a strong base.

But there are worries. Amendments to forest laws in 2023, fast-tracked clearances and diversion of forest land for projects have raised concerns about weaker scrutiny. Projects such as the Ken–Betwa river link will submerge part of the Panna Tiger Reserve; the Great Nicobar project will clear tropical forest in a biodiversity-rich island. The challenge is not whether to develop but how.

Reconciling the two

The answer lies in smart, sustainable development:

  • Avoid, minimise, mitigate: avoid the most valuable habitats, and route roads and rail lines around them.
  • Green infrastructure: animal underpasses and overpasses, as on NH-44 through the Pench landscape, and speed limits on railway lines in elephant corridors.
  • Landscape planning: protect corridors that link reserves, not just islands of forest.
  • Honest environmental impact assessment with public hearings and independent monitoring.
  • Community partnership: recognise forest rights, share tourism revenue, and pay quick compensation for crop and livestock losses, so that local people become guardians of wildlife.
  • Compensatory afforestation that restores real ecosystems, not monoculture plantations.

Conclusion

Gandhi said the earth provides enough to satisfy every man's need, but not every man's greed. Wildlife preservation and development are not enemies; both aim at a better life for people. A growing India must build infrastructure, but it must build with care, so that the tiger, the elephant and the forests that sustain us all survive into the India of 2047.
free.ifm-2025-ge-1c:
PrivacySurveillancePuttaswamyProportionality

Freedom in the Age of Digital Surveillance

Every tap on a phone leaves a trace. Our location, purchases, searches, faces and voices are recorded by apps, cameras and governments. Digital technology has given us great freedom to speak, learn and trade, but it has also created tools of surveillance more powerful than any earlier ruler possessed. The question is whether freedom can survive when everything can be watched.

The two faces of digital technology

On one side, technology has empowered citizens. UPI, Aadhaar-based delivery of benefits and online public services have reached millions who were left out. Social media lets ordinary people question the powerful and organise. On the other side, the same data can be used to watch, profile and control. CCTV networks with facial recognition, mass data collection by apps, spyware such as Pegasus, and the tracking of activists and journalists in many countries show the darker side.

How surveillance threatens freedom

Surveillance changes behaviour. When people know they are watched, they speak less, read less and protest less — the chilling effect. Dissent, which democracy needs, is quietly suppressed. Data can be used to discriminate: credit, jobs and insurance may be denied on the basis of opaque algorithms. Data breaches expose private lives. In authoritarian states, digital surveillance has been used to monitor whole communities. Private companies, too, practise "surveillance capitalism", selling attention and shaping choices through targeted content.

The Indian framework

India's Supreme Court, in K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), held that privacy is a fundamental right under Article 21, and that any intrusion must pass the test of legality, legitimate aim, proportionality and procedural safeguards. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and its rules (2025) give individuals rights over their data and impose duties on companies. Yet concerns remain: the Act gives the government wide exemptions, interception under the Telegraph and IT laws is authorised by the executive without judicial approval, and independent oversight is weak. The Pegasus case led the Supreme Court to appoint a technical committee, showing both the seriousness of the issue and the difficulty of holding surveillance to account.

Is all surveillance bad?

No. States must fight terrorism, cybercrime, child abuse and fraud, and targeted, lawful surveillance helps. CCTV can make streets safer for women. The issue is not whether there is surveillance, but whether it is necessary, proportionate, authorised by law and subject to independent review.

Protecting freedom

  • Strong laws and oversight: judicial or independent approval for interception, parliamentary oversight of intelligence agencies, and public reports on surveillance requests.
  • Data protection in practice: a truly independent Data Protection Board, purpose limitation and data minimisation.
  • Privacy by design: encryption, limited data retention and audits of facial-recognition systems.
  • Digital literacy: citizens who understand permissions, privacy settings and their rights.
  • Accountability of platforms for misuse of data and opaque algorithms.

Conclusion

Benjamin Franklin warned that those who give up essential liberty for a little temporary safety deserve neither. In the digital age, the choice is not between security and freedom; a society can have both if power is checked. Technology should serve citizens, not watch them. The test of a democracy in the twenty-first century is whether it can use data for the common good while keeping the private life and free voice of every citizen safe.

Impact of Artificial Intelligence on the Employment Sector

Every great technology has raised the same fear: that machines will take away human work. The power loom, the tractor and the computer each destroyed some jobs and created many more. Artificial intelligence is different in one way — it can do not only physical tasks but also mental ones: writing, translating, coding, diagnosing and advising. Its impact on employment will therefore be deeper and faster.

How AI is changing work

AI automates routine tasks, both manual and cognitive. Chatbots handle customer queries, software reads documents and invoices, and algorithms screen loan applications and job candidates. Generative AI drafts reports and code in seconds. The International Monetary Fund estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide, and about 60% in advanced economies, are exposed to AI. Exposure does not always mean loss: in many jobs AI will complement workers, making them more productive, while in others it may replace tasks.

Jobs at risk

The most vulnerable are routine white-collar jobs: data entry, basic accounting, call centres, simple programming and back-office work. This matters for India, whose IT and business-process services employ millions. In manufacturing, AI-driven robots may reduce the advantage of low-cost labour on which developing countries have relied.

New jobs and opportunities

At the same time, AI creates demand for data scientists, AI engineers, cyber-security experts, prompt designers and people who train, check and maintain AI systems. It can raise productivity in agriculture (crop advisories, pest detection), health (early diagnosis in rural areas), education (personalised learning) and governance (faster delivery of services). The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report expects both large job creation and displacement this decade, with a net gain, but with very different skills required.

The Indian context

India has a large, young workforce and a strong digital public infrastructure. The IndiaAI Mission (2024) aims to build computing capacity, datasets and AI skills. India could become a global centre for AI services. But most Indian workers are in the informal sector with low skills, and women's participation in the workforce is low. If AI benefits only a small, skilled elite, inequality will widen.

Challenges

  • Skill mismatch: workers whose tasks are automated may not easily move to new roles.
  • Inequality: gains may go to capital and big technology firms rather than workers.
  • Gig work: AI-driven platforms manage delivery and ride-hailing workers through algorithms, often without social security.
  • Bias and fairness in AI-based hiring.

What must be done

  • Reskilling and lifelong learning: Skill India and Digital India programmes must teach AI, data and digital skills, and the NEP 2020's focus on critical thinking and vocational education must be implemented.
  • Human-centred adoption: use AI to augment workers — doctors, teachers and farmers — rather than simply cut jobs.
  • Social security: the Code on Social Security covers gig and platform workers; it must be implemented well.
  • Support for small firms and startups to adopt AI.
  • Ethical regulation for transparency and fairness in AI used for hiring and work.

Conclusion

AI is neither a job destroyer nor a job creator by nature; its impact depends on how societies prepare. If India invests in skills, safety nets and responsible use, AI can lift productivity, raise wages and create new kinds of work. If it does not, AI may deepen unemployment and inequality. The future of work will belong not to machines alone but to people who learn to work with them.

  • Water bodies and wetlands act as heat sinks (blue-green infrastructure).
  • Permeable surfaces reduce stored heat and flooding.
  • Co-benefits: cleaner air, groundwater recharge, biodiversity and better health.

Limits and complements

Green infrastructure needs space and water, and works best with cool roofs (reflective paint), energy-efficient buildings (ECBC), better urban design and heat action plans such as Ahmedabad's (2013).

Green infrastructure is therefore a key, low-cost and sustainable part of the answer to urban heat, though it must be combined with other measures.

1. Himalayan and Peninsular rivers compared

2. Inter-linking of rivers

The National Perspective Plan (1980) proposed 30 links (14 Himalayan, 16 Peninsular) to move surplus water to deficit basins. The Ken–Betwa link is the first under way (foundation stone 2024).

3. Possible consequences

  • Positive: irrigation for about 35 million hectares, drought and flood moderation, hydropower, drinking water and inland navigation.
  • Ecological: submergence of forests and wildlife habitat (Panna Tiger Reserve under Ken–Betwa), changes to river flows and less sediment reaching deltas, saline intrusion.
  • Social: displacement of people, loss of livelihoods.
  • Economic: very high cost and long gestation; questions about whether "surplus" basins really have surplus in dry years.
  • Federal and international: disputes among States and with Nepal and Bangladesh over Himalayan links.

Inter-linking must be judged project by project, with careful environmental and social assessment, while cheaper options such as watershed development, groundwater recharge and efficient irrigation are pursued.

White RevolutionOperation FloodBlue RevolutionPMMSY

White Revolution: the rapid growth of milk production through Operation Flood (1970–1996) under Dr Verghese Kurien and the NDDB, built on the Anand cooperative model. India is now the world's largest milk producer (about 239 million tonnes in 2023-24).

Blue Revolution: the growth of fisheries and aquaculture, through the Blue Revolution scheme (2015) and the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana (2020). India is the world's second-largest fish producer.

Can they transform rural livelihoods? Yes, to a large extent:

  • Income for small and landless households: dairying gives daily cash income; most milk comes from small herds.
  • Women's empowerment: women do most dairy work and lead many cooperatives and fisheries self-help groups.
  • Nutrition: milk and fish improve protein intake.
  • Risk reduction: income that does not depend only on crops.
  • Jobs in processing, cold chains and exports (shrimp, marine products).

Conditions: fodder and feed shortages, animal disease, low productivity of cattle, overfishing and pollution must be tackled through cooperatives, credit (Kisan Credit Cards for animal husbandry and fisheries), veterinary care and sustainable aquaculture.

DharaliFlash floodDebris flowFragile Himalaya

On 5 August 2025 a sudden flood and debris flow in the Kheer Ganga (Kheer Gad) stream swept through Dharali village in Uttarkashi district, on the Gangotri route, burying homes, hotels and markets.

Natural causes

  • Steep, young Himalayan slopes with loose glacial and landslide debris.
  • Intense rain in the upper catchment; the event was first called a cloudburst, though rain gauges recorded modest rainfall, and experts also pointed to the collapse of moraine or ice and a landslide-dammed pool upstream.
  • Narrow valleys that funnel water and debris at high speed.

Human-made causes

  • Construction on the stream's old debris fan and flood plain: hotels and shops built in the path of past floods.
  • Unplanned growth for Char Dham tourism; road cutting and slope disturbance.
  • Weak early warning and poor hazard zoning.
  • Climate change, which makes extreme rain and glacier melt more frequent.

Lessons: hazard mapping and no-build zones on flood fans, carrying-capacity limits for tourist towns, early-warning systems and Doppler radars, and slope-safe road design.

The Dharali flood shows that natural triggers turn into disasters when people build in the path of floods.

Indian agriculture is adopting new technologies to raise yields, cut costs and cope with climate change.

1. Digital agriculture

  • Digital Agriculture Mission (2024) and AgriStack: a digital registry of farmers and crops; crop surveys from satellites.
  • AI-based advisories on weather, pests and prices (for example Kisan e-Mitra and the National Pest Surveillance System).
  • e-NAM online markets and digital payments.

2. Precision and smart farming

  • Drones for spraying fertiliser and pesticides (the Namo Drone Didi scheme for women's groups).
  • Sensors and IoT for soil moisture; soil health cards.
  • Micro-irrigation (drip and sprinklers) under Per Drop More Crop.

3. Better inputs

  • Nano-urea and nano-DAP to cut fertiliser use.
  • Biofortified and climate-resilient varieties; the first genome-edited rice varieties (2025).
  • Natural and organic farming (National Mission on Natural Farming, 2024).

4. Mechanisation and post-harvest

  • Custom hiring centres, small machines for small farms.
  • Cold chains, solar dryers and food-processing units.

Challenges: small holdings, cost of technology, digital literacy and data privacy. FPOs, custom hiring and extension services can spread these technologies to small farmers.

Ecosystem servicesLivelihoodsCarbon sinkISFR 2023

Forests are the natural capital of a nation: they produce goods, sustain life and protect the economy.

1. Economic wealth

  • Timber, fuel, fodder, bamboo and non-timber forest produce (tendu leaves, honey, lac, medicinal plants).
  • Livelihoods for an estimated 27 crore people who depend on forests.
  • Eco-tourism and industries such as paper, furniture and herbal medicine.

2. Ecological wealth (ecosystem services)

  • Water security: forests feed rivers and recharge groundwater.
  • Soil protection against erosion and landslides.
  • Climate regulation: India's forests store about 7,285 million tonnes of carbon (ISFR 2023) and help meet the NDC target of an extra 2.5–3 billion tonnes CO2-equivalent sink.
  • Biodiversity: habitats for tigers, elephants and countless species; India has four biodiversity hotspots.

3. Social and cultural wealth

  • Homes and identity of tribal communities; sacred groves; traditional knowledge.

4. Present position

Forest and tree cover is 25.17% of India's area (ISFR 2023), below the 33% goal of the National Forest Policy, 1988; degradation and fragmentation continue.

The statement is therefore justified: forests are wealth that grows if managed sustainably and is lost for generations if destroyed.

Biotechnology uses living organisms and their enzymes to produce clean energy and to clean up pollution.

Energy management

  • Bioethanol: fermentation of sugarcane, grains and crop residue (second-generation ethanol, such as the Panipat plant); India reached close to 20% ethanol blending in petrol in 2025.
  • Biogas and compressed biogas from cattle dung and waste (GOBARdhan, SATAT).
  • Biodiesel from non-edible oils; algal biofuels under research.
  • Microbial fuel cells that produce electricity from waste water.

Pollution control

  • Bioremediation: microbes that break down oil spills and pesticides; phytoremediation with plants.
  • Biological treatment of sewage (activated sludge) and biofilters for gases.
  • Biodegradable plastics (PLA) and enzymes that break down PET.
  • Bio-fertilisers and bio-pesticides that cut chemical use.

The BioE3 policy (2024) promotes such bio-manufacturing for a green economy.

Greenhouse gasesFossil fuelsDeforestationFeedback loops

The Earth's average temperature has risen by about 1.2–1.3 °C above pre-industrial levels, and 2024 was the first year above 1.5 °C (WMO).

Reasons

  • Burning fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) for power, industry and transport — the main source of CO2, now above 420 ppm.
  • Deforestation and land-use change, which remove carbon sinks.
  • Agriculture: methane from rice fields and livestock; nitrous oxide from fertilisers.
  • Industry: cement, steel and fluorinated gases (HFCs).
  • Waste: methane from landfills.
  • Feedback loops: melting ice lowers reflectivity (albedo); thawing permafrost releases methane; warmer seas absorb less CO2.

Natural factors such as solar cycles and El Niño cause short-term swings, but the IPCC finds that human activity is the main cause of the warming since 1950.

SuperpositionEntanglementQubitNational Quantum Mission

Quantum mechanics explains nature at the atomic scale; quantum technologies use its strange rules — superposition and entanglement — to compute, communicate and sense in new ways. Moving from theory to devices is a real "quantum leap".

(i) Classical mechanics versus quantum mechanics

(ii) Classical bit versus quantum bit

  • A bit is 0 or 1.
  • A qubit can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 at the same time, and qubits can be entangled, so their states are linked. n qubits can represent 2ⁿ states together.
  • Qubits are fragile and lose their state through decoherence, so they need very low temperatures or isolation.

(iii) Supercomputer versus quantum computer

  • A supercomputer uses thousands of classical processors in parallel; it is reliable and general-purpose (India's PARAM series).
  • A quantum computer uses qubits and interference to solve certain problems — factorising, simulating molecules, optimisation — far faster than any classical machine. It is still error-prone and not a replacement for all computing.

India's effort: the National Quantum Mission (2023), ₹6,003.65 crore up to 2030-31, aims at 50–1,000-qubit computers, quantum communication and sensors.

Grid balancingPumped storageLithium-ionRenewables

Need and importance

Solar and wind power vary with time of day and weather, while demand peaks in the evening. Electrical energy storage stores surplus power and releases it when needed.

  • Balances supply and demand and keeps grid frequency stable.
  • Allows more renewable energy (India's target: 500 GW non-fossil capacity by 2030).
  • Cuts peak-time costs, provides backup and powers electric vehicles.

(i) Hydroelectric (pumped) storage

  • Two reservoirs at different heights.
  • When power is cheap or in surplus, water is pumped up to the upper reservoir — electrical energy is stored as gravitational potential energy.
  • At peak demand, water flows down through turbines, generating electricity.
  • Efficiency about 70–80%; large capacity and long life, but needs suitable sites.

(ii) Electrochemical storage (batteries)

  • Energy is stored as chemical energy through redox reactions.
  • In a lithium-ion battery, lithium ions move from cathode to anode during charging and back during discharge, while electrons flow through the external circuit.
  • High efficiency (about 90%), fast response and modular, but cost, limited life and mineral supply are concerns. Sodium-ion and flow batteries are alternatives.

India supports storage through viability-gap funding for battery storage, the PLI scheme for advanced chemistry cells and guidelines for pumped-storage projects.

Feynman 1959Top-downBottom-upSurface-to-volume ratio

In 1959 Richard Feynman said "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom": matter could be arranged atom by atom. Nanotechnology works at 1–100 nanometres, where materials gain new properties.

(i) Top-down and bottom-up fabrication

  • Top-down: cutting bulk material down to the nanoscale — lithography (as in computer chips), etching, ball milling.
  • Bottom-up: building structures from atoms and molecules — chemical vapour deposition (carbon nanotubes, graphene), sol-gel methods, self-assembly.

Bottom-up is closer to Feynman's vision of arranging atoms.

(ii) Surface-to-volume ratio

  • As particles get smaller, a larger share of their atoms lie on the surface: a 1 cm cube cut into 1 nm cubes has ten million times more surface area.
  • Surface atoms are more reactive, so nanoparticles are better catalysts, sensors and drug carriers.
  • Quantum effects change colour, strength and conductivity — gold nanoparticles look red, and nano-silver kills microbes.

Thus there is indeed "plenty of room at the bottom" for new materials and devices.

Scientific temperArticle 51A(h)EclipsesAnti-superstition laws

Science replaces belief without evidence with explanation that can be tested. Article 51A(h) makes developing a scientific temper a fundamental duty.

(i) Myths about eclipses

  • Myth: the demon Rahu or Ketu swallows the Sun or Moon; food cooked during an eclipse is impure; pregnant women should stay indoors.
  • Science: a solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth; a lunar eclipse when the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon. They are predictable to the minute. The only real risk is eye damage from looking at the Sun without filters.

(ii) Superstitious treatment of illness

  • Exorcism, black magic, branding and "witch-hunting" instead of medical care delay treatment of epilepsy, mental illness, snakebite and infections, sometimes causing death.
  • Science explains disease through germs, genes and lifestyle and treats it with tested medicine and vaccines.

Steps

Science education, health awareness by ASHA workers, and laws such as Maharashtra's anti-superstition law (2013) and Karnataka's (2017).
